Max-heap: one structure, two pictures

 i — selected
 ⌊i/2⌋ — parent
 2i, 2i+1 — children Click any tree circle or array cell: the same item lights up in both views, with its parent and children. Hover an edge or arc to see its heap-property test.
⚠ Figure failed to load

plan.contextChunk: This figure pairs two views of the same max-heap, labeled (a) on the left and (b) on the right. Panel (a) is a binary tree of ten gray circles joined by straight edges, with the value inside each circle and a smaller index printed just above and outside it. The root holds 16 at index 1; its children hold 14 at index 2 and 10 at index 3; the node 14 has children 8 at index 4 and 7 at index 5; the node 10 has children 9 at index 6 and 3 at index 7; the node 8 has children 2 at index 8 and 4 at index 9; and the node 7 has a single left child, 1 at index 10, so the bottom level is filled only from the left. Panel (b) is a horizontal row of ten gray boxes reading 16, 14, 10, 8, 7, 9, 3, 2, 4, 1 from left to right, with the indices 1 through 10 written above them. Curved arcs above and below the row connect each cell to the two cells that hold its children, which always lie further right. Setting the branching picture beside the flat row shows that the same parent-child relationships survive the change of representation. The figure introduces the array form of a heap, in which moving between a node and its children reduces to arithmetic on the index.

interactionPlan.concept: A max-heap is simultaneously a nearly-complete binary tree and a flat array: index arithmetic (parent = ⌊i/2⌋, children = 2i and 2i+1) replaces pointers, while the heap property A[parent] ≥ A[child] governs the values.
elements: Panel label '(a)' centered beneath the left tree
Panel label '(b)' centered beneath the right array
Left panel: binary tree of 10 gray-filled circles with black outlines, value centered inside each circle
Small index numeral printed above-outside each circle (1..10), not inside it
Node 5 (value 7) has only a left child, so the bottom level is filled left-to-right with a gap on the right
Right panel: single horizontal row of 10 gray boxes with black borders, values 16, 14, 10, 8, 7, 9, 3, 2, 4, 1 left to right
Index labels 1..10 printed above the array row
Curved arcs above the array linking each cell i to its children 2i and 2i+1 for the upper-level nodes (1→2,3; 2→4,5; 3→6,7)
Curved arcs below the array linking cells 4→8,9 and 5→10
Heap size annotation A.length = A.heap-size = 10
Highlight styles: selected node/cell (strong accent fill), parent (secondary accent), children (tertiary accent)
Readout panel showing current i, value A[i], parent index ⌊i/2⌋, child indices 2i and 2i+1 with 'none' when out of range
Comparison badges A[parent] ≥ A[child] shown on edges/arcs in the heap-property view

interactions.teaches: The tree circle and the array cell are the same object: clicking either one lights up the matching item plus its parent and children in BOTH views, so the two pictures are one data structure.
Navigation in a heap is pure arithmetic — sweeping i shows ⌊i/2⌋, 2i, 2i+1 tracking the true parent and children, and going out of range exactly where the tree runs out of nodes.
interactions.label: Index i

interactions.teaches: Structure and value order are independent claims: the arcs/edges show WHERE things sit, the comparison badges show that every parent's value dominates its children's.
interactions.label: Overlay

demo_steps.title: Two pictures, one heap
demo_steps.narration: On the left a binary tree, on the right a flat array — but the values read off level by level, left to right, are identical: 16, 14, 10, 8, 7, 9, 3, 2, 4, 1. The arcs on the array show the tree edges hiding inside the row.

demo_steps.title: The root and its children
demo_steps.narration: With i = 1, the children are at 2i = 2 and 2i + 1 = 3 — cells 14 and 10, exactly the root's two tree children. There is no parent, since ⌊1/2⌋ = 0 falls outside the array.

demo_steps.title: Climbing up: parent = ⌊i/2⌋
demo_steps.narration: At i = 5 the parent index is ⌊5/2⌋ = 2, and indeed the node holding 7 hangs below the node holding 14. Both 4 and 5 map back to the same parent 2 — integer division folds two children into one parent.

demo_steps.title: Where the tree runs out
demo_steps.narration: At i = 5 the children would be 10 and 11, but the heap size is 10, so node 5 has only a left child. Sweep further to i = 6 or beyond and both child indices exceed the array — those are the leaves.

demo_steps.title: The max-heap property
demo_steps.narration: Switch the overlay to value order: every edge now carries A[parent] ≥ A[child]. 16 ≥ 14, 14 ≥ 8, 8 ≥ 4 — the largest element sits at the root, but siblings like 7 and 9 are in no particular order.

demo_steps.title: Layout and order together
demo_steps.narration: Showing both overlays at once separates the two ideas: index arithmetic decides who is whose child, and the heap property constrains only the values along those parent-child links — never across the array left to right.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The tree edges are never stored — they are computed: a node at index i finds its parent at ⌊i/2⌋ and its children at 2i and 2i+1, which is why a heap needs no pointers at all.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Two side-by-side panels on white. LEFT (a): a four-level binary tree of gray (#D9D9D9) circles with black strokes, value in large type inside, small index numeral in italic-ish serif just above-left/above-right outside the circle; straight thin black edges; the bottom level is filled left to right with node 10 (value 1) as the only child of node 5, leaving an obvious gap on the right. RIGHT (b): a row of ten equal gray boxes with black borders, values 16 14 10 8 7 9 3 2 4 1, index numerals 1..10 above; thin curved arcs, drawn above the row for parents 1–3 and below the row for parents 4–5, each connecting a cell to its two children further right. Panel captions '(a)' and '(b)' centered below each. Highlight palette: selected = saturated orange fill, parent = blue fill, children = green fill, applied to the matching circle AND the matching array cell simultaneously, with the connecting edge/arc thickened. A small readout box near the array reports i, A[i], PARENT(i)=⌊i/2⌋, LEFT(i)=2i, RIGHT(i)=2i+1, graying out entries that exceed heap-size 10. In 'Heap property' mode, replace/augment the links with small comparison badges like '16 ≥ 14' on each edge and arc, colored green since all hold.

authoredContext: The (binary) heap data structure is an array object that we can view as a nearly complete binary tree (see Section B.5.3), as shown in Figure 6.1. Each node of the tree corresponds to an element of the array. The tree is completely filled on all levels except possibly the lowest, which is filled from the left up to a point. An array A that represents a heap is an object with two attributes: A:length, which (as usual) gives the number of elements in the array, and A:heap-size, which represents how many elements in the heap are stored within array A. That is, although AŒ1 : : A:length may contain numbers, only the elements in AŒ1 : : A:heap-size, where 0 _x0014_ A:heap-size _x0014_ A:length, are valid elements of the heap. attempts.html:
Max-heap: tree ⇄ array

Click any tree circle or array cell to select it — the match lights up in both views, with its parent and children.
⚠ Figure failed to load

discrepancies: Default (step 0) state is not gray like the source: the root cell/circle is orange and nodes 2 and 3 (and their array cells) are green, so the figure does not read as a drop-in replacement for the static image until the user changes state.
Tree index numerals for nodes 9 and 10 collide (label for 9 is placed right of its circle at x≈196, label for 10 left of its circle at x≈204), rendering as an unreadable '9 10' blob.

Extra chrome absent from the source: a colour legend under the tree and a boxed PARENT/LEFT/RIGHT readout panel beside the array; both use ~12–13px text inside a 1200-wide viewBox that is downscaled ~50%, so they render at ~6px and are effectively illegible.

Overall scale/composition: the 1200×500 viewBox leaves large empty bands above and below, shrinking the tree, array and all numerals well below the source's visual weight (node values ~10px on screen vs. large bold numerals in the source).
Array index numbers (1–10) sit far above the row (y=132 vs. cell top at 215), a much larger gap than in the source where they sit just above the arcs/cells.
evaluation.notes: Topology, arc placement and captions faithfully reproduce the CLRS heap tree/array pair and the interactions (index slider, overlay select, demo steps, click-to-select) are genuinely useful, but the default state is pre-highlighted in orange/green rather than the source's uniform gray, node labels 9 and 10 overlap, and the added legend/readout text is far too small at inline size.

feedback.rationale: The conceptual decomposition and interaction structure are correct; the issues are implementation-level (default highlight colors, overlapping index labels, tiny legend text, viewBox scale/spacing), which the generator should fix.

Max-heap: one structure, two pictures

 i — selected
 ⌊i/2⌋ — parent
 2i, 2i+1 — children Click any tree circle or array cell: the same item lights up in both views, together with its parent and children.

discrepancies: Index numerals beside the tree nodes are offset by a fixed rule (even indices left, odd right) rather than following the incoming edge as in the source; consequently label '5' sits to the right of node 7 and label '6' to the left of node 9, crowding the two numerals together, whereas the source places both to the upper-left of their nodes.

The array index labels 1–10 are placed well above the cell row (≈56px gap) instead of snugly above the boxes as in the source, and when the readout panel appears they sit on/overlap its bottom border.

Array linking arcs are all uniform quadratic curves of similar height; the source shows a wider variety of nested arc spans (including a long above-row arc reaching index 10), so the arc pattern is only approximate.

Overall drawing is scaled fairly small inside a tall viewbox, leaving a large blank region below the figure; node values (~13px effective) and index numerals (~10px effective) are noticeably smaller relative to the frame than in the source.

Added elements not in the source: coloured highlight fills, a boxed PARENT/LEFT/RIGHT readout panel, and 'A[p] ≥ A[c]' badges on every edge/arc (only shown after interaction, but the 9 badge pairs can crowd the small tree in 'Heap property' mode).
evaluation.notes: A faithful, well-structured recreation of the CLRS heap tree/array pair with excellent, conceptually apt interactions (index slider, overlay modes, linked click selection, 6-step narration); weaknesses are small-scale rendering with excess whitespace, a couple of index-label placement choices that crowd or drift from their cells, and one narration slip calling 7 and 9 'siblings' when they are cousins.
action_items: Place tree index numerals on the side of the incoming edge (as the source does) so labels 4/5 and 6/7 don't crowd each other, and move the array index labels closer to the top of the cell row while re-routing the above-row arcs to clear them.
Tighten the viewbox (reduce empty space below the figure) and/or enlarge node radius and font sizes so values and index numerals stay comfortably legible at inline width.
Ensure the readout panel does not overlap the array index numerals — shift it up or reserve a clear band between panel and labels.
Fix the step-5 narration: 7 and 9 are cousins, not siblings; use an actual sibling pair (e.g. 8 and 7, or 2 and 4) to illustrate that siblings are unordered.
In 'Heap property' mode show comparison badges only for the currently highlighted parent–child links (or on hover) to avoid nine overlapping labels on the small tree.

feedback.rationale: The concept and interaction structure are sound; remaining issues are concrete rendering fixes (label placement, viewbox scaling, panel overlap, badge density, one narration wording), which belong to the generator.

demo_steps.narration: At i = 5 the parent index is ⌊5/2⌋ = 2, and indeed the node holding 7 hangs below the node holding 14. Both 4 and 5 map back to the same parent 2 — integer division folds two children into one parent.

demo_steps.title: Where the tree runs out
demo_steps.narration: At i = 5 the children would be 10 and 11, but the heap size is 10, so node 5 has only a left child. Sweep further to i = 6 or beyond and both child indices exceed the array — those are the leaves.

demo_steps.title: The max-heap property
demo_steps.narration: Switch the overlay to value order: every edge now carries A[parent] ≥ A[child]. 16 ≥ 14, 14 ≥ 8, 8 ≥ 4 — the largest element sits at the root, but siblings like 7 and 9 are in no particular order.

demo_steps.title: Layout and order together
demo_steps.narration: Showing both overlays at once separates the two ideas: index arithmetic decides who is whose child, and the heap property constrains only the values along those parent-child links — never across the array left to right.

plan.keyInsight: The tree edges are never stored — they are computed: a node at index i finds its parent at ⌊i/2⌋ and its children at 2i and 2i+1, which is why a heap needs no pointers at all.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Two side-by-side panels on white. LEFT (a): a four-level binary tree of gray (#D9D9D9) circles with black strokes, value in large type inside, small index numeral in italic-ish serif just above-left/above-right outside the circle; straight thin black edges; the bottom level is filled left to right with node 10 (value 1) as the only child of node 5, leaving an obvious gap on the right. RIGHT (b): a row of ten equal gray boxes with black borders, values 16 14 10 8 7 9 3 2 4 1, index numerals 1..10 above; thin curved arcs, drawn above the row for parents 1–3 and below the row for parents 4–5, each connecting a cell to its two children further right. Panel captions '(a)' and '(b)' centered below each. Highlight palette: selected = saturated orange fill, parent = blue fill, children = green fill, applied to the matching circle AND the matching array cell simultaneously, with the connecting edge/arc thickened. A small readout box near the array reports i, A[i], PARENT(i)=⌊i/2⌋, LEFT(i)=2i, RIGHT(i)=2i+1, graying out entries that exceed heap-size 10. In 'Heap property' mode, replace/augment the links with small comparison badges like '16 ≥ 14' on each edge and arc, colored green since all hold.

discrepancies: Tree node spacing is much tighter than the source: bottom-row circles (2, 4, 1) nearly touch and the index numerals '8', '9', '10' collide with the circles/edges instead of sitting clearly above-left/above-right as in the original.

Node 5 (value 7) and node 6 (value 9) circles are almost touching in the generated tree, whereas the source leaves a clear gap between the left and right subtrees; the whole (a) panel reads more cramped than the source.

Index numerals above the array cells and above the tree nodes render very small at inline size (≈10px effective), noticeably less prominent than the source, where they are near the same weight as the cell values.

Array arcs are drawn as single quadratic Béziers of uniform curvature; the source shows nested arcs of visibly varied heights (e.g. 1→2 tight, 3→7 wide) — minor stylistic difference but arcs are slightly flatter/more overlapping than the original.
An extra readout box (i / PARENT / LEFT / RIGHT lines) appears over the top-right of the drawing when any control is used — not present in the source (correctly hidden at step 0).
evaluation.notes: Structurally faithful two-panel reproduction (tree + array with parent/child arcs) with genuinely useful interactions — index slider, overlay mode, 6-step narrated demo, and click-to-link-both-views — but the tree layout is cramped so several index numerals collide with circles, and all index labels are uncomfortably small at inline size.
action_items: Widen horizontal spacing of the tree (especially the bottom level and the gap between the left/right subtrees) or shrink node radius so circles never touch and index numerals sit clearly outside the circles.

Increase index-numeral font size (and the array index row) relative to the viewbox so they are comfortably legible inline, and offset leaf labels further from the incoming edge to remove the '8'/'9'/'10' collisions.
Vary arc heights in panel (b) so nested parent→child arcs (1→2, 1→3, 2→4, 2→5, 3→6, 3→7) stack without overlapping, matching the source's layered look.
Reposition the interaction readout box below the array or inside the side panel so it never overlaps the (b) panel artwork.
